question: What information do you think the coding agent gathers before it makes a change, and how does it get that information?
How do you think the agent decides which steps to take and which files to change?
How was the agent's underlying model trained, and what does it rely on to know about your specific project?
When did the agent make a wrong change or get stuck, why do you think that happened, and what factors had the greatest impact?
How should an agent's changes and actions be reviewed, approved, and verified?
How well do you understand how the AI programming tools you use work?
options: Not at all
Slightly
Moderately
Very well
Extremely well

question: During the task, what did the agent use to decide what to do?
options: Your typed request
Files it opened and read with its tools
Output of commands it ran, such as test results
Everything on your computer, automatically
Details of your goal that you never wrote down
correct_answers: Files it opened and read with its tools
Output of commands it ran, such as test results
explanation: The agent only knows what you tell it and what its tools bring back. It cannot see anything else.

question: Your project has 500 files. Before editing, how does the agent know what's in them?
options: It already has the whole project memorized
It searches for and opens the files it judges relevant, one step at a time
It downloads your project from GitHub
It reads every file each time you send a message
correct_answers: It searches for and opens the files it judges relevant, one step at a time
explanation: The agent can hold only a limited amount at once, so it reads selectively and can miss a relevant file.

question: You give the same request, “add a discount function”, twice. The first time the project has a rules file (such as CLAUDE.md or .cursorrules) that says “round money with Math.round”; the second time it doesn't. What happens?
options: The code differs, because the rules file becomes part of the agent's context
The code is the same, because agents ignore project files
The code is the same, because the agent remembers its first answer
The agent asks which version you prefer
correct_answers: The code differs, because the rules file becomes part of the agent's context
explanation: Instructions in project files are read into the context and shape every step that follows.

question: The agent writes a test, runs it, sees it fail, fixes the code, and reruns it until it passes. What does this show?
options: It understands your program the way an experienced developer does
It repeats a loop: predict an action, observe the result, predict the next action
It looked up the fix online
A person at the company fixed it remotely
correct_answers: It repeats a loop: predict an action, observe the result, predict the next action
explanation: Running tools and reading their output lets a prediction-based model correct itself. That is feedback, not human-like understanding.

question: You ask the agent to “make checkout faster”. How does it choose which files to change?
options: It finds the provably optimal change
It predicts a plausible plan from your request and the files it has read, which may not be the best plan
It changes every file in the project
It picks files at random
correct_answers: It predicts a plausible plan from your request and the files it has read, which may not be the best plan
explanation: The plan is a prediction. A vague request gives the agent more room to choose a direction you didn't intend.

question: How did the agent's model gain its coding knowledge?
options: Before release, by training on large amounts of code and text, including examples of using tools
By learning each time it runs your tests
Engineers wrote rules for every programming task
By saving the projects of users whose code was correct
correct_answers: Before release, by training on large amounts of code and text, including examples of using tools
explanation: Training happens ahead of time. During your task the model's weights do not change.

question: A library was released yesterday. Can the agent use it correctly?
options: Yes, it already knows every library
Only if it reads the documentation, through a web search tool or files you give it; otherwise it may guess
Yes, it retrains overnight
No, an agent can never use new information
correct_answers: Only if it reads the documentation, through a web search tool or files you give it; otherwise it may guess
explanation: The model's own knowledge stops at its training cutoff. Tools can bring newer information into its context.

question: Yesterday you corrected the agent: “use pytest, not unittest.” Today you start a new session. Will it remember?
options: Yes, the model retrained on your correction
Only if the correction was saved to a memory or rules file, or you resume the same conversation
Yes, it always remembers everything you say
No, there is no way to carry it over
correct_answers: Only if the correction was saved to a memory or rules file, or you resume the same conversation
explanation: Memory comes from text that gets reloaded into context, not from the model learning.

question: The agent confidently uses an API option that doesn't exist. Why?
options: It copied the option from a website it just visited
It produced a plausible-looking pattern from its training data without checking the real documentation
It was optimizing for the shortest code
It reused another user's stored code
correct_answers: It produced a plausible-looking pattern from its training data without checking the real documentation
explanation: Confident output is not the same as verified output. The agent can invent details that look right.

question: The agent says, “All tests pass.” Which statements are true?
options: The code is now guaranteed to be correct
Tests check only what they test, so untested behavior could still be wrong
The agent may have changed the tests themselves to make them pass
Agents cannot run tests
correct_answers: Tests check only what they test, so untested behavior could still be wrong
The agent may have changed the tests themselves to make them pass
explanation: Passing tests is evidence, not proof. Always check what was tested and whether the tests were changed.

question: The agent asks permission to delete the build/ folder and edit six files. What should you do?
options: Read the command and the changes before approving
Approve everything, because the AI knows best
Run the tests yourself and check that the result matches your goal
Rewrite your request more clearly if the plan doesn't match your intent
correct_answers: Read the command and the changes before approving
Run the tests yourself and check that the result matches your goal
Rewrite your request more clearly if the plan doesn't match your intent
explanation: The agent acts, but you are accountable for what it changes. Permission prompts exist so you can check its work.
